q: Why does a smaller barrel exert more influence on the wine?
opts: It is always made of newer wood
It has more surface area for its volume
It is stored at higher temperature
exp: More wood touches less wine, so both flavour extraction and slow oxygen ingress work faster. A 225 litre barrique marks wine far more than a large old cask.

q: How does American oak typically differ from French oak in flavour?
opts: American contributes more tannin and less aroma
American tends to give more overt vanilla and coconut
exp: American white oak is generally more overt, with vanilla, dill and coconut notes, while French oak tends toward finer spice and subtler texture.

q: What does toasting a barrel refer to?
opts: Heating the staves over fire during shaping
Rinsing the barrel with hot water before filling
Charring the outside of the barrel to preserve it
Seasoning the staves outdoors before the barrel is built
exp: Bending staves over fire also transforms the wood chemistry. The toast level a cooper applies changes the aromatic contribution considerably.

q: A base wine is bottled with yeast and sugar, and the carbon dioxide produced stays trapped in that same bottle. Which method is described?
exp: Base wine is bottled with yeast and sugar, and the second fermentation happens in that same bottle, trapping the carbon dioxide and leaving lees behind.

q: What is the tank method, also called Charmat, used for?
opts: Fortifying the wine with neutral grape spirit
Running the second fermentation in a sealed tank
Ageing red wine on oak staves inside a steel tank
Freezing wine in the tank to concentrate it
exp: The second fermentation runs in a pressurised tank and the wine is filtered and bottled under pressure. It is faster and cheaper, and it preserves primary fruit aromas.

opts: Turning bottles gradually to settle lees
Adding the yeast and sugar for the second fermentation
Removing the plug of sediment from the neck
exp: After riddling drives the lees into the neck, that plug is frozen and ejected by internal pressure. The bottle is then topped up before final closure.

q: The dosage is added at which point, and does what?
opts: Before the first fermentation, to raise alcohol
During riddling, to clarify the wine
exp: The liqueur d'expedition tops up the bottle after disgorgement and sets the sweetness level, from brut nature through to doux.

q: Extended ageing on the lees contributes which character?
exp: Autolysis, the breakdown of the spent yeast cells, releases compounds giving brioche, biscuit and toast, and builds texture. Time on lees is the main lever for that character.

q: Port is fortified at which point?
opts: At bottling, once ageing is finished
Before fermentation begins, in the must
exp: Neutral spirit is added while sugar remains, killing the yeast and stopping fermentation. That is why Port is both sweet and high in alcohol.

opts: A film of yeast that grows on the surface of the wine
A sweetening agent added to Sherry at bottling
exp: Flor is a living yeast veil that grows on wine in partly filled butts, shielding it from oxygen and giving Fino and Manzanilla their distinctive tang.

q: Wine is drawn from the oldest tier of casks and topped up from the next youngest, on down the scale. What is this called?
exp: Wine is drawn from the oldest tier and replaced from the next youngest, on down the scale. The result is a consistent blend that carries a fraction of much older wine.

q: A producer waits for a hard freeze, picks fruit still frozen on the vine and presses it solid. Which style is being made?
exp: Pressing naturally frozen grapes leaves water behind as ice and releases concentrated sugary juice. It demands a hard freeze on fruit still hanging.

q: The passito or appassimento method involves
opts: fortifying the must partway through fermentation
adding unfermented must to finished wine
fermenting the wine under a veil of flor yeast
exp: Grapes are dried on mats or racks, losing water and concentrating everything left. Amarone and Vin Santo are made this way.

q: Why does noble rot concentrate sweetness?
opts: It converts the berry's acid into extra sugar
It punctures the skin so water evaporates
It adds sugar of its own into the pulp of the berry
exp: Botrytis threads pierce the skin and the berry dehydrates, concentrating sugar, acid and flavour while contributing its own honeyed character.

q: A wine smells of damp cardboard and wet cellar, and its fruit seems stripped out. Which compound is the most likely cause?
exp: TCA gives damp cardboard and wet dog, and strips a wine of its fruit. It can arrive by cork but also through contaminated cellar materials.

q: Which fault presents as vinegar and nail polish remover?
exp: Volatile acidity is largely acetic acid with ethyl acetate. Tiny amounts add lift; past a threshold the wine smells of vinegar and solvent.
